> SUP-29410 ticket record: "priority: P1 / severity: Sev2 / status: Closed / updated_at: 2026-02-04" (closed to the customer, yet the later-dated matrix of 2026-02-21 still shows ❌ for Python streaming timeouts).

**Freshest status** (`sdk-parity-audit-working-notes` §25 p5; Slack `1768467711`, `1768602215`):

> "4) Python streaming timeouts not honored - Priority: P0 - Status: in progress - Owner: Sabrina - PR: py#850 + py#854"
> "3) Retry-After ignored (Go) - Priority: P0 - Status: in review - Owner: Mateusz - PR: go#612"
> "2) Retry classification retries on 400 (TS) - Priority: P0 - Status: fixed pending release - PR: ts#1298"
> Slack: "Sahana Iyer: conformance suite just went red on main for TS + Go. failing case is `streaming_429_retry_after_respected`" — root cause "Dana Lo: TS streaming path returns an AsyncIterable from a function that does: `const res = await fetch(url, { signal })` … so it never hits `withRetry()`"; "Mateusz Zielinski: Retry-After parsing isn't wired into the streaming transport."
> Post-beta Slack (`1768602215`): "Go status: conformance: currently red on one case: `Retry-After` http-date parsing with timezone"; "TS: green"; "Python: conformance green on main + release branch"; "still seeing some streaming disconnects behind enterprise proxies"; Allison Grant: "If Go still lacks Retry-After date parsing, that's a no-go for stable tag IMO."

## Answer

The v1 standard requires: `overall_timeout_ms` (90s) as a hard cap implemented via an outer timer/abort even when the HTTP client can't express it, `stream_idle_timeout_ms` (30s, reset on every valid chunk/event) still bounded by the overall cap, retries capped at `max_attempts=4` / `max_total_retry_time_ms=20000` with full-jitter exponential backoff (250ms→8s), Retry-After honored on 429 (always) and 503 in both seconds and HTTP-date form clamped to 0–60s with no jitter on top, retries only on 408/429/5xx and transport errors (never 400/401/403/404/409/422), and **no automatic retry once any streaming output has been delivered** (typed disconnect error carrying request_id, bytes/events received, partial-output flag, attempt count).

Yes, violations remain on all three SDKs, with Go and Python the clearest: **Go** ignores Retry-After outright (matrix ❌; SUP-29477) and is still conformance-red on HTTP-date parsing post-beta, plus inconsistent streaming idle timeout and unbounded connect timeout when no context is set; **Python** still ignores `timeout` in the streaming iterator path (matrix ❌, audit item "in progress", SUP-29410/SUP-29505 "timeout applied to initial request but not subsequent read loop"), plus 3-vs-4 max attempts, 60s overall default, and missing HTTP-date parsing; **TypeScript**'s 400-retry bug is "fixed pending release" (ts#1298) but its streaming path historically bypassed the retry wrapper entirely (429 thrown with retry_count=0), it can treat post-content disconnects as retryable network errors, and its streaming idle timeout is "not implemented."

## 1. What to emit for an Optimization Config rollback

**Event names** — all namespaced under `optimization_config.*`, format `optimization_config.<noun>.<verb>` (`optimization-config-audit-events` · §2 · p3):

> "Event names are namespaced under: `optimization_config.*`"

Rollback section of the taxonomy (p3):
- `9) optimization_config.rollback.requested` — "Emitted when a rollback is initiated (Console button/API)."
- `10) optimization_config.rollback.executed` — "Emitted when rollback is executed and control plane considers the rollback applied (per rollback semantics)."
- `11) optimization_config.rollback.failed` — "Emitted when rollback cannot be executed."

The same spec's "Required field mapping by event" table (p4) also carries the rollout-shaped rollback names:

| Event | Additional required fields |
|---|---|
| `optimization_config.rollback.started` | `rollout_id`, `from_version_id`, `to_version_id` |
| `optimization_config.rollback.gate_evaluated` | `rollout_id` |
| `optimization_config.rollback_paused` | `rollout_id` |
| `optimization_config.rollback.completed` | `rollout_id`, `to_version_id` |
| `optimization_config.rollback.failed` | `rollout_id`, `error_code` |
| `optimization_config.rollback.requested` | `from_version_id`, `to_version_id` |
| `optimization_config.rollback.executed` | `from_version_id`, `to_version_id` |
| `optimization_config.rollback.failed` | `from_version_id`, `to_version_id`, `error_code` |

Per-event semantics (p3): for `rollback.requested`, "`from_version_id` = currently active version at time of request", "`to_version_id` = requested prior version", "`result` may be `success` or `failure`", "SHOULD include `reason`"; for `rollback.executed`, "`result` = `success`".

**Required fields (MUST) on every event** (`optimization-config-audit-events` · §2 · p2 — "All Optimization Config audit events MUST include the required fields below."):

## 2. If the rollback succeeds in Console but never appears in the customer's SIEM export

This is exactly ticket **SUP-18544** (Northbridge Analytics, Sev2/P1): "Optimization Config rollback actions are not appearing in their audit log export / SIEM pipeline. Rollback itself succeeds… Apply/promote events show up as expected."

Triage checklist from the ticket (§10):
1. "Confirm rollback happened in Console history and in control-plane event logs."
2. "Verify whether event was emitted but dropped by exporter (schema mismatch / missing required fields)."
3. "Verify taxonomy match vs documented event names in Confluence."
4. "Confirm whether rollback endpoint path uses the same audit emitter as apply/promote."

**Root cause found in this incident (§12/§13):** "the rollback endpoint emitted a non-taxonomy event name (`optimization_config.rollback`) and omitted required schema fields, causing the audit-export pipeline allowlist/schema validation to drop the event." Confirmed by: "audit-exporter allowlist includes `optimization_config.rolled_back` but not `optimization_config.rollback`" and "rollback endpoint payload omits `previous_config_version` (it only includes target_version). Exporter schema validation requires both for optimization config changes, otherwise it drops the event." Fix: rename to the taxonomy-compliant name, add `previous_config_version`, `new_config_version`, `scope`, always-present `request_id` + actor identity, plus an integration test asserting the exporter receives rollback events.

So check, in order: (a) emitted at all vs emitted-but-dropped; (b) `event_name` exactly matches the registered/allowlisted taxonomy name; (c) all required before/after version fields + `request_id` + actor present (schema validation drops otherwise); (d) producer parity — does the rollback endpoint use the same emitter as apply/promote; (e) if emitted and valid but not delivered, switch to the delivery path (`audit-log-pipeline-incident-runbook`): exporter queue depth/error rate per tenant+destination, Kafka `audit.events.v1` consumer lag and `audit.events.dlq`, p95 `audit_e2e_latency_seconds`, then "Verify the destination endpoint and credentials/token… Confirm the destination is accepting requests from Redwood's egress IPs… trigger a re-export for the affected window." The coverage runbook's decision tree says the same: "Yes → Likely missing required fields or unregistered `event_type`. Fix in code + add test." Note also that export can legitimately lag — Console should show a UI note that "audit event may be delayed by export pipeline", and post-fix delivery was "within 60–90s".

**Naming caveat worth flagging:** the canonical spec page uses `optimization_config.rollback.requested/executed/failed`, while the SUP-18544 thread cites the taxonomy page as expecting `optimization_config.rolled_back` (past tense) with required `action`/`result`, and the working sheet uses `rollback.requested/completed/failed`. Reconcile against the live exporter allowlist before emitting — a mismatch is precisely what dropped the event.

## Answer

**SLO targets (fast tier, Hosted US/EU):** p95 ≤ 350 ms and **p99 ≤ 700 ms** for short prompts; **streaming TTFT p99 ≤ 450 ms**. (standard: p95 ≤ 900 ms / p99 ≤ 1800 ms; cost-efficient: p95 ≤ 1800 ms / p99 ≤ 3500 ms.)

**Abort criteria for a fast-tier p99 regression in canary:**
- **Hard abort → immediate rollback + hold:** fast tier p99 > SLO target × 1.15 for 10 m in any canary region for top-3 models, refined to **trigger if (p99 > target×1.15) OR (p99 > baseline×1.20) for 10 m**. Supporting hard-abort signals: 5xx > baseline + 0.3% for 5 m; **scheduler admission rejects > 2% for 10 m**; **queue depth > 3× baseline for 15 m AND rising**; GPU OOM > 0.1%/10 m; cancels+timeouts > baseline + 0.5% for 10 m with GPU util > 90%.
- **Soft abort → pause ramp + investigate:** **fast tier TTFT p99 regression > 10% for 15 m even if overall p99 is not tripped**; `reason_code=MODEL_CONSTRAINT_FALLBACK` > 5%; `reason_code=unexpected_tier_mapping` spikes; tier-label cardinality > 2× baseline for 15 m; support-ticket spike.
- Fast-tier p99 abort **pages** (per paging policy); the perf-canary gate stays failing until a baseline is re-approved or the metric returns within threshold — do not refresh baselines to clear it.

**Rollback steps (in order):**
1. Set `tiered_batching_defaults_enabled=false` (global kill switch at control plane; per-route override available to pin legacy batching).
2. Verify propagation on the control-plane status page (expected < 2 m).
3. Confirm `reason_code=TIER_DEFAULT` drops to ~0 in canary regions.
4. If latency hasn't recovered in 10 m, also restore `scheduler.max_wait_ms` to the legacy default via emergency override.
5. Post to #incidents (if customer impact) + #eng-sre summary.
6. If p99 hasn't returned within 15 m post-rollback, treat as a separate incident and keep defaults off until RC. Narrower alternative: roll back fast-tier defaults only for the affected model/region cohort.

**Dashboards to confirm admission control vs. requeue:**
- `grafana.redwoodinference.com/d/batching-tiers/canary-tiered-batching` — the canary tiered-batching dashboard (direct deep-links `viewPanel=12`, `18`, `27` for latency / queue depth / error); watch p50/p95/p99 by tier/model/region, **queue depth, admission rejects, `max_wait_ms` hit rate**, batch_tokens distribution, cache hit/evictions.
- **Tiered Batching — Queue & Backpressure** panel (queue depth, queue wait time, admission-control rejects, shed counts, overload-mode indicator) and **Tiered Batching — Regression Triage** (current-vs-baseline p95/p99 deltas, top offenders by tier/model family/region), plus **Latency & Streaming** split by tier and streaming vs non-streaming (PR-933 pack).
- `grafana.redwood.inference/d/perf-canary/fast-tier` (perf-canary fast-tier dashboard, e.g. `?var-model=qwen2.5-32b-instruct&var-region=us-east-1`, panel 42) for the gate itself.
- Decision rule: **queue depth + time-in-queue rising with latency → overload/backpressure (admission control)**; **queue depth flat while p99 rises → scheduler/kernel regression, model-level issue, or downstream gateway**. Also rule out telemetry artifacts first (tier-label cardinality blow-up, PR-28544 hotfix precedent).

**Reason codes / metrics to use:**
- Scheduler/admission: `WAIT_BUDGET_EXCEEDED`, `PREFILL_BATCH_LOCKED`, `REQUEUE_DEADLINE_BOOST`, `overload_admission_block`, `overload_shed`.
- Tier selection: `tier.default.fast|standard|cost_efficient`, `tier.override.route_policy`, `tier.override.customer`, `tier.constrained.model_limit`, `tier.overload_mode.active`, `tier.fallback.compat_variant`, plus `TIER_DEFAULT`, `MODEL_CONSTRAINT_FALLBACK`, `unexpected_tier_mapping`.
- Metrics: fast-tier **admission rejects** and **wait-budget drops** (PR-28458), `max_wait_ms_hit_rate`, and `scheduler_fast_requeue_boost_total{model,tier,region}`.
- Requeue signature to look for in traces: `admit=false reason=WAIT_BUDGET_EXCEEDED ... action: requeue priority=normal` repeating — the known canary cause was PR-28458's fast-tier wait budget + admission control requeuing at normal priority, causing requeue storms/priority inversion behind long prefills (fast-tier p99 1180 ms → 1715 ms, +45%, qwen2.5-32b only; did not reproduce with `scheduler.fast_tier.admission_control=false`). Mitigations: cut prefill batch early when `oldest_wait_ms > 0.75*max_wait_ms`, and deadline-aware requeue priority (`scheduler.fast_tier.deadline_requeue_boost=true`, canary-only).

## Concise answer

**Check first:** pin the pool key `<region>/<hardware_class>`, then on the **Neighbor Impact** dashboard compare non-burst vs burst latency deltas and tail amplification ratio, check whether the global/region circuit breaker or `NeighborImpactGateTriggered` is already active, and break denials down by `reason_code` to see whether one top-talker tenant, a tier cohort, or global load is driving it (also check telemetry freshness and router/scheduler queue depth — the shared routing path, not burst spillover, is the usual culprit).

**Reduce burst caps first** (least-disruptive): as soon as non-burst latency SLO is regressing or baseline errors increase, tighten/enable the Neighbor Impact Gate and reduce burst for the pool — lower `max_burst_ratio`, clamp per-tenant caps for top talkers, raise cooldowns; disable burst for the pool if still regressing.

**SLO gate** is the automated version: REDUCE after ~3 minutes of regression (clamps `max_burst_ratio`, e.g. 2.0 → 1.2), DISABLE at a higher threshold or after `disable_after` (default 10m); exits after 10m below `exit_threshold`.

**Circuit breaker** is the hard stop: use it when non-burst p95 has been above the SLO threshold for >10 minutes correlated with burst activity (unless there's a fast fix), or when pool stability/admission-controller health is at risk or neighbor impact persists — enable it for the affected `<region>/<hardware_class>`, and if it's already enabled and instability continues, disable the burst feature flag for the pool and set max burst ratio to 0. Escalate immediately if non-burst regression persists >15 minutes.

**Denial reason code:** burst customers get HTTP 429 with **`NEIGHBOR_SLO_GATE`** (burst reduced/disabled to protect non-burst SLOs) in the `x-redwood-burst-denial-reason` header — `TENANT_CAP_REACHED` if a cap clamp bites them, `FLEET_SAFETY_CAP` if the breaker/fleet cap engages; internally the gate records `SLO_GATED`. ## Why some Hosted API overload errors were missing `Retry-After`

**The header was only emitted by one of several places that can produce an overload response — the gateway's own admission-control/overload handler.** The primary incident is `SUP-2860-retry-after-header-missing-on-overload-responses` ("# Retry-After header missing on some overload (503/429) responses for Hosted API (enterprise tenant)", Sev2/P1, Aurora Health Systems, prod us-east + eu-west, §1).

- Customer symptom (§3): *"Aurora Health Systems reports that when they receive overload responses (503 / occasionally 429) from Hosted API, the Retry-After header is not present on some routes. Their client relies on Retry-After for backoff; without it they either retry too aggressively (risking retry storms) or back off too conservatively…"*
- Gateway engineer Amara Diallo (§12): *"admission-control middleware sets Retry-After on overload rejects it generates. However, when upstream service returns a 503 overload JSON, we currently do not normalize/add Retry-After unless the error is produced by the gateway overload handler. Needs a post-processing step for overload-classified errors from downstream."*
- Overload-protection owner Christine Wong correlated it (§12): *"customer requests were shed both at gateway (token bucket) and at runtime saturation (queue depth). Only gateway sheds had Retry-After. This matches customer report (embeddings had 429 w/ header; chat had 503 w/o header)."*
- Recorded root cause (§13): *"Retry-After header was only set for overload responses generated directly by gateway admission-control. Overload responses originating from downstream routing/runtime returned the correct overload JSON payload but were passed through without header normalization."* (Hypothesis in §10: *"downstream returns a structured JSON error but does not set headers; gateway sometimes passes body through without applying header normalization."*)

The same gap showed up independently elsewhere: the gateway rate-limiter path "sets 429 but Retry-After is inconsistent (sometimes absent)" (`1767938855` §2); header was set on overload-breaker sheds but "there was an edge case when the request was rejected downstream (after routing) where header did" not appear (`1743608844` §2); and a game day found "~7% of 503 overload responses missing Retry-After header on the streaming route (likely gateway path mismatch)" (`ENG-4830-game-day-overload-simulation` §11, with Christine Wong noting "only /v1/chat.completions with stream=true on one gateway path", §14). It was tracked as a standing support-facing known issue: "Symptom: Customer receives 429/503 overload payload but no Retry-After" (`overload-errors-and-retry-guidance` §5).

## Changes that made it consistent across gateway, routing, and streaming

**1. Gateway normalization hotfix — PR-18472 (linked to SUP-2860).** Amara Diallo "Implemented hotfix to apply Retry-After for any response classified as `overload_error` by error mapper (regardless of origin), unless Retry-After already set. Also ensures x-redwood-request-id present" (`SUP-2860` §12). The PR "standardizes how we emit Retry-After and correlation IDs for overload/load-shedding responses… to keep behavior stable across gateway/routing/runtime," and specifies: *"Retry-After is now set for all overload-class responses emitted by the API gateway (admission control + breaker open + dependency brownout mapping) and for propagated overload errors from downstream services when they bubble back through the gateway"* (`pr-18472-load-shedding-retry-after-and-client-guidance` §2). Construction was "centralize[d] … into a shared helper that sets headers + JSON payload consistently (status, error.code, error.message, retry guidance, request_id)".

**2. Routing path explicitly covered.** Reviewer Mina Haddad asked "On routing fallback, we sometimes return an overload from routing with a retryable code. Are we certain Retry-After is preserved when routing returns its own error payload?" — resolved: *"Gateway now overwrites/sets Retry-After on mapped overload regardless of downstream body, but preserves downstream error.code/message"* (§3).

**3. Guardrail so it doesn't leak onto non-overload errors.** Ethan Park: *"do not add Retry-After to non-overload 5xx; only apply when stable overload code is detected (e.g., overloaded, breaker_open, dependency_overloaded)"* (`SUP-2860` §12); enforced by "a guard test to ensure generic 5xx errors do not set Retry-After" (`pr-18472` §3). Same constraint in the failover work: "Retry-After is only emitted for overload/circuit-breaker conditions (not for generic 5xx)" (`pr-19820-api-gateway-fallback-timeout-tuning` §5).

**4. Streaming path.** Because headers can't be added mid-response, PR-18472 §2 states: *"For streaming (SSE) requests, we only attempt overload rejection before the response is committed; once headers have been sent, we cannot reliably add Retry-After. This PR ensures the admission decision happens before initiating the stream in gateway,"* validated by an "Integration test covering /v1/chat/completions streaming: overload rejection happens before stream start and includes Retry-After + request id" plus a "Regression test for SUP-2860 reproduction (route missing header)". Mid-stream failover now "return[s] a terminal frame that includes an error code and Retry-After guidance; clients should reconnect" (`pr-19820` §5). Later work closed the remaining streaming gaps: the OpenAI-compat overhaul "Normalize[s] Retry-After handling and response codes… Both endpoints include Retry-After (seconds or HTTP-date) and a structured JSON error with a stable error_code" (`pr-52100-streaming-retry-idempotency-overhaul` §2), and the published streaming contract requires clients to "obey service-supplied Retry-After or Rate-Hint headers when present" (`streaming-error-taxonomy-and-retry-contract-2026` §2).

**5. 429 / rate-limit + error-shape parity follow-on (ENG-5130).** Platform ticket "Gateway: standardize Retry-After + error shape fields for SDK classification" required "Ensure gateway emits Retry-After on *all* 429s that are due to rate limiting / quota enforcement" and "header is present for both standard JSON responses and streaming initiation failures", because "429 responses omit Retry-After or use inconsistent formats" and "streaming errors don't include the same identifiers/shape as non-streaming" (`ENG-5130-platform-retry-after-and-error-shape-consistency` §3–§4). Implementation: "on 429 from rate-limit service, inject Retry-After if missing. For upstream 429s, will preserve Retry-After if present; otherwise compute from limiter window reset" (§10), shipped as `pr-28411-api-gateway-add-retry-after-on-429` ("consistently emit Retry-After on 429 responses + align SDK error fields"). Earlier graceful-degradation work added the "gateway: add overload response helper + Retry-After header plumbing" and "metrics: add overload_response_total + retry_after_seconds histogram" (`pr-19827-add-graceful-degradation-retry-after` §7–§8). SDKs then map the header: "sdk/http: map response payload + Retry-After header into error instances" (`pr-418-expose-overload-error-types` §7), and docs were updated after "Confirmed gateway will emit Retry-After consistently post pr-18472. Please include fallback behavior if header missing (older regions during rollout)" (`ENG-4832-sdk-docs-update-for-retry-guidance` §8).

**6. Rollout.** "Shipped via hotfix PR-18472 and rolled out progressively (staging → us-east canary → us-east+eu-west full)" (`SUP-2860` §13), behind the `overload_protection.retry_after_normalization` flag at 5% of tenants, ending with "Rollout complete: 100% prod us-east + eu-west. Verified in logs for Aurora tenant: overload 503 responses now include Retry-After: 1–3 seconds (bounded)" (§12). ENG-5130 used "staged rollout (1% -> 10% -> 100%)" and reported "429_missing_retry_after dropped to ~0" (§7, §10).

## Alerts and safeguards that keep it consistent

- **Dedicated missing-header metric + alert hook.** Aisha Bello (review): *"Please add a metric for missing Retry-After as a canary safety check. We should be able to alert if this regresses."* → *"Added api_gateway.overload.retry_after_missing counter (dimensions: route_group, region, status) and wired it into logging when helper isn't used (should stay at 0)"* (`pr-18472` §3). ENG-5130 added `gateway_429_missing_retry_after_count` "in the rollout dashboard to ensure we're not regressing", alongside monitoring of "429 rate + client retry rates (risk: retry storms)", "distribution of Retry-After values", "error response schema validation sampling", and "request_id missing rate (target: 0)" (§10, §7).
- **Canary verification and close criteria.** "Monitoring canary: no increase in 5xx, shed rate unchanged, p99 stable. Confirmed headers present in sampled logs for overload responses (gateway + downstream)" (`SUP-2860` §12); ticket close gate: "Monitor for 72 hours; close if no further reports of missing Retry-After on overload responses" (§1).
- **Runbook instrumentation.** The overload runbook has a dedicated triage step "### 4) Address missing Retry-After / bad error payloads", tracks "Retry-After missing rate" as a key metric before/after each change, lists "Missing Retry-After/correlation ID" among post-incident follow-up issues to file, and reminds oncall to "Ensure consistent `Retry-After` to prevent retry storms" (`hosted-overload-circuit-breaker-runbook` §4).
- **Support escalation path.** "Symptom: Customer receives 429/503 overload payload but no Retry-After… Action: Escalate if reproducible; include route + correlation IDs" (`overload-errors-and-retry-guidance` §5).
- **Semantic drift alert.** "Add telemetry exposing mismatch between Retry-After header and effective tenant refill window (support dashboard alert)" (`SUP-101999-priority-inversion-retry-after-smoothing-explainer` §16).
- **Release gates / conformance.** SDK-parity release gate requires "Platform prerequisites confirmed shipped": "API gateway emits Retry-After on 429", "request_id consistently present on error responses (streaming + non-streaming)", "error code enum stable for SDK classification", plus dashboards for "429 rate and Retry-After compliance proxy" and "request_id presence rate in errors" (`release-checklist-sdk-parity` §3); verification asks to "Verify gateway emits Retry-After consistently on 429 for both streaming and non-streaming paths" (`SUP-29477-go-sdk-missing-retry-after-handling-429` §12).
- **Client-side contract.** "Clients should respect Retry-After when present, use exponential backoff with jitter as a fallback, and avoid unbounded retries to prevent retry storms" (`SUP-2860` §13).

**In short:** `Retry-After` was missing because it was attached only where the gateway's own admission-control/overload handler generated the response; overload responses produced downstream (routing/runtime, streaming paths, and some rate-limiter paths) came back as valid overload JSON bodies that the gateway passed through without header normalization. PR-18472 fixed this by centralizing overload-response construction so the gateway stamps `Retry-After` (integer seconds) plus correlation IDs on *any* overload-classified response regardless of origin — gated on a stable overload code so non-overload 5xx are untouched, with the streaming admission decision moved before the stream is committed — and later work (PR-28411/28426/28440 under ENG-5130, PR-19827, PR-19820, PR-52100) extended the same guarantee to all 429s, mid-stream failover frames, and SDK error mapping. Consistency is now protected by `retry_after_missing` counters wired to canary alerting, sampled-log verification, staged rollouts, 72-hour post-fix monitoring, runbook metrics/escalation steps, a Retry-After-vs-refill-window dashboard alert, and SDK-parity release gates.

## Why observed canary % in one region can diverge from the Console rollout step

**The Console step is the *desired* state; the data plane serves whatever rollout config each router pod last successfully applied.** In the canonical incident, the divergence was a **stale-config / watch-disconnect problem confined to one region**:

- `SUP-48377-canary-traffic-split-not-matching-config` · §1 · p1 — title: *"Hosted canary rollout: traffic split in us-east not matching Console config (canary receiving ~25% when set to 10%)"*
- §3 · p1 — *"Customer reports that the canary cohort is receiving substantially more traffic than configured for a Hosted route rollout. Console shows canary set to 10% (after being reduced from 25%), but observed canary traffic remains ~22–27% in us-east."*
- §9 · p2 — the routing decision log shows the two values disagreeing directly: *"configured_canary_percent=25 (unexpected)"* vs *"console_step_target_percent=10 (expected)"*
- §10 · p2 — *"Smart Routing in us-east is using a stale rollout config (still at 25%) after a step change to 10% was applied in Console/control plane."*
- §15 · p3 — *"root cause was a router config watch disconnect in us-east; some pods did not re-connect and continued serving an older rollout step (25%)"*; *"Seeing configured_canary_percent=25 for rollout rll_9f3c2d3a on a subset of pods. Others show 10. This is consistent with watch stream disconnect + no periodic resync."*

The runbook generalises this into a symptom class — `runbook-rollout-stuck-or-bad-split` · §2 · p2: *"Split matches overall, but **per-region** mismatch (e.g., us-east OK, eu-west off)"*, with likely causes *"Multi-region propagation lag (config not yet applied everywhere)"*, *"Data plane caching old route config"*, *"Deterministic cohort key mismatch (unexpected hashing input due to missing user/session key)"*, *"Sticky assignment changes across retries"*, and *"A/B test or fallback routing policy taking precedence (policy evaluation order)"*. Its triage table maps the single-region case exactly: *"Only one region mismatched | Propagation / region-specific dataplane | Route config apply status in that region"* (§2 · p3). Policy can also skew one region: *"Region routing constraints may redirect canary traffic to baseline in some regions"*, *"Quota/rate limiting policy may shed canary disproportionately"* (§2 · p5).

Also note the benign explanation: §2 · p3 — *"At low volumes, small absolute differences look like large % differences… Deterministic cohorting can produce slight variance at very low traffic; treat >2–3x deviation (or persistent deviation >15 minutes) as suspicious."* The customer-facing how-to adds *"Region skew (tenant traffic is concentrated in a region not fully deployed)"* and *"Request stickiness key mismatch (client not sending stable key)"* (`how-to-enable-hosted-canary-rollouts-for-a-tenant` · §24 · p5).

## Recommended oncall mitigations

1. **Safe pause first** — runbook §2 · p4: *"Pause rollout from Console (preferred; ensures audit event): Console → Hosted Route → Rollouts → Select rollout → **Pause**… Confirm in orchestrator that state is PAUSED and no scheduled transitions remain."*
2. **Rollback if unsafe** — §2 · p2: *"If splits are clearly unsafe (e.g., canary unexpectedly at ~100%): **Rollback immediately**"*; §2 · p5, for a region with partial apply: *"If canary receiving unintended traffic in that region: rollback."*
3. **Fix the split without rollback (low impact only)** — §2 · p4: *"1) **Re-apply step / re-sync config** — Trigger a 'reconcile/apply' action in orchestrator… Confirm apply ack in every region. 2) **Lower canary percent** — If canary is receiving more than expected, reduce target to a safe value (e.g., 0–1%)… 3) **Pause and hold**."*
4. **Concrete stale-config action (what actually worked)** — SUP-48377 §11 · p2: *"restart/roll router deployment in us-east OR force a full config resync"*, and §15 · p3: *"Mitigation: rolling restart of router-canary + router-stable deployments in us-east to force fresh config pull. ## Answer

**Event names being standardized.** SDK/docs examples and golden fixtures must use one canonical, provider-neutral event vocabulary. The conventions page ("Canonical event types (examples MUST use these names)") fixes: `response.started`, `message.delta`, `message.final`, `tool_call.delta`, `tool_call.final`, `response.completed` (the only success terminal), `response.error`, `response.interrupted`. The ADR's "Canonical event names used in examples" table carries the same lifecycle with `.done`-style spellings — `message.delta`, `message.done`, `tool_call.delta`, `tool_call.done`, `response.done`, `error` — so the two governing docs agree on the *lifecycle* (delta → final/done per message and per tool call, plus a single success terminal and an error event) while the terminal/final names still drift (`.final`/`response.completed`/`response.error` vs `.done`/`response.done`/`error`); the conventions page explicitly warns against "Mixing provider-specific event names in docs."

**Fields being standardized.** Every event is an envelope with at least `type`, `request_id`, and a type-specific payload (optionally `event_id`, `model`, `created_at`, `usage`). Tool-call fields: `tool_call_id` (the sole key for the accumulator map), `name` (may arrive early, late, or be omitted on later deltas — cache it), `arguments_delta` (ADR) / `delta.args_fragment` (conventions) for the streaming fragment, accumulated into `arguments_buffer` / `args_text`, and the final `arguments` as a **complete JSON string** — never a JSON object mid-stream. Args are an opaque string during streaming; parse/validate only at `tool_call.final`/`tool_call.done`, never on a delta, and never run the tool before then. Parallel calls are assembled independently per `tool_call_id` because deltas interleave. Golden fixtures assert a stable sequence of canonical event types (not raw provider fields) plus the final assembled message text and tool-call args, and must include a case with args fragmented across multiple `tool_call.delta` events.

**Mapping OpenAI-compatible tool-call deltas.** Treat the compat stream as a source to be reframed into the canonical model, not as a 1:1 contract:
- `choices[].delta.content` fragments → `message.delta` (`content_delta` appended to the per-message buffer); terminal/`finish_reason` → `message.final` + `response.completed`/`response.done`.
- First appearance of `tool_calls[]` with `id` + `function.name` (internal `tool_call_start`) → open a `tool_call.delta` for that `tool_call_id`, setting `name` (equivalently a tool-call start signal).
- Subsequent `tool_calls[].function.arguments` string fragments (internal `tool_call_chunk`) → `tool_call.delta` with `arguments_delta`, appended to that id's buffer. Do not parse; the fragments are not valid JSON and may split mid-token or carry whitespace/escapes.
- `tool_call_end` / completed call (or `finish_reason: tool_calls`) → `tool_call.final`/`tool_call.done` carrying `tool_call_id`, `name`, and the assembled `arguments` JSON string; parse once and validate against the tool schema, then enqueue execution.
- Route every fragment by `tool_call_id` (falling back to OpenAI's `index` only to establish identity), never "the latest tool call", so interleaved parallel calls stay separate and ordering is preserved; if the stream ends without a final/done, treat args as incomplete and retry or error clearly.
- `metadata` frames and `finish_reason` map to response-level envelope/terminal fields, not to argument assembly. Per the ADR, docs must state that the compat payload "may contain additional fields and may not be byte-for-byte identical", with SDK adapter helpers doing this mapping.

## Canonical contract: ADR‑022 — HTTP 409 + `residency_policy_violation`

The canonical contract is **ADR‑022 "Error contract for residency violations"** (`adr-022-error-contract-for-residency-violations`, §2, p.1–3). It "defines the **public-facing error contract** returned when a request is blocked by **Hosted data residency region pinning**," and states that the contract is used by "**API Gateway enforcement (pre-routing)**, Smart Routing (as a defensive backstop; must not return divergent formats), SDKs (Python/TS/Go) mapping to a dedicated error type."

**1) HTTP status** — p.1–2: "**HTTP 409 Conflict**". Rationale explicitly rejects the alternatives: "403 Forbidden conflates authorization vs. policy configuration and is commonly retried/handled incorrectly," "422 Unprocessable Entity is typically reserved for semantic payload validation." The Context section names your exact symptom: "Different endpoints returned different status codes (403/409/500)" and "**Streaming paths sometimes returned generic 500s after the connection was established**."

**2) Canonical error envelope** — p.2: "All residency blocks MUST use the standard Redwood error envelope," with top-level key `error`; `error.code` stable and machine-readable; `error.request_id` matches `x-redwood-request-id`; `error.help_url` points to public docs; `error.details` bounded and non-sensitive. Required in `error`: `message`, `code`, `subcode`, `request_id`, `help_url`. Required in `error.details`: `allowed_regions`, `candidate_region`, `policy_scope` (`"org" | "project" | "api_key"`); optional `primary_region`, `policy_id`. Headers: `x-redwood-request-id: <req_...>` (always present) and `content-type: application/json`.

**3) Error codes** — p.2: "`error.code = \"residency_policy_violation\"`", with stable subcodes `"region_not_allowed"`, `"primary_region_unavailable"`, `"policy_misconfigured"`.

**7) Streaming endpoints behavior** — p.3, the clause that governs your bug: "Residency enforcement MUST occur **before any streaming bytes are written**." … "If the request is blocked, the server MUST return **HTTP 409** with the standard JSON error body (i.e., do not start the stream)." Non-compliant behavior is listed explicitly: "returning HTTP 200 and then emitting an ad-hoc \"error\" SSE event", "**returning a generic 500 mid-stream**", "closing the connection without a structured error."

**8) Retry semantics** — p.3: "Clients/SDKs MUST treat `residency_policy_violation` as **non-retriable by default**."

**9) SDK surface requirements** — p.3: "Create a dedicated, typed exception (name by language): **Python: `ResidencyPolicyViolationError`** … Include fields/properties: `code` (always `residency_policy_violation`), `subcode`, `message`, `request_id`, `help_url`, `allowed_regions`, `candidate_region`, `primary_region` (optional), `policy_scope`, `policy_id` (optional). Preserve the raw HTTP status (409) and headers for debugging."

Implementation note (p.4): "**Gateway is the enforcement source of truth for formatting.** Downstream services may attach structured context for logs/metrics but MUST NOT craft customer-facing payloads. Routing may detect a violation as a backstop. If so, it must return the same envelope/fields."

## Where it is enforced — API Gateway

**Final answer**

When a new Sev0/Sev1 incident is created with `incident_type = unknown`:

- **Immediate workflow (owner):** "Unknown" is permitted but explicitly **not a final state**. The IC must **assign primary owner = SRE (Reliability) temporarily**, post a note in the incident channel stating what is known, what is unknown (missing signals), and **the time classification will be revisited**. Pager routing also falls back to **SRE primary** with an annotation so on-call can reclassify. Unknown may not be used to dodge team ownership or to delay paging.
- **When it must be reclassified:** classification is required within **10 minutes** of declaration for Sev0/Sev1; the SLA side grants a **15-minute "classification grace period"** (60 min for Sev2/Sev3) after which the incident is treated as `incident_type = "unknown"`. The IC must **revisit at T+30 min and T+60 min** from incident start, and if still unknown at the second checkpoint must pull in the **SRE Duty Manager** to arbitrate and pick the "least-wrong" category. If reclassification changes the owner, the new owner on-call must be engaged immediately (and the change announced in-channel).
- **SLA timers in the meantime:** the SLA clock is **not paused** — it starts at declaration (`incident.created_at`) once severity is set, and after the grace period the evaluator runs against **conservative/default SLA targets for `incident_type = "unknown"`, keyed to tier + severity**, until the type is updated. (Severity changes later recompute due times from the original start, with an audit-log entry.)
- **Alerts in the meantime:** warning/breach alerting keeps firing on those default targets — **T-30m and T-10m warnings for the Sev0/Sev1 mitigation target (TTM), T-60m for the fix target (TTF)**, plus the Sev0/Sev1-only **"Remediation SLA breached"** alert (`breach="true", severity=~"Sev0|Sev1"` over 15m, `For: 0m` — pages immediately, routing to the **Incident Commander + owning team on-call**, i.e. SRE while the owner is still the temporary one). Note the rollout default in PR-28635 is **Slack-only with paging disabled** unless `remediation_sla.paging_enabled` is on. Separately, unknown/unclassified creation spikes (≥2 in 1h) raise a non-paging `#eng-sre` alert, and classification-compliance drops below 0.95 alert to `#eng-sre`/`#oncall-sre`.

## Answer

**Start in `observe` mode, not `enforce`.** For the runtime 1.19 Dedicated canary, the TP watchdog ships `runtime.tp_watchdog.enabled = false` by default and runs in `mode: "observe"` (soft-only: log + increment metric, no abort/drain) on perf-canary plus one Dedicated canary cluster. Only after the false-positive rate is validated do you flip to `"enforce"` for the 5% Dedicated canary. Operationally the checklist is stricter still: keep the watchdog OFF for the first 30–60 minutes after deploy (approval thread says off for the first 10% canary, enable after ~2 hours if error budget is clean), turn it on for one shard/one cluster first, and observe 30 minutes of trigger count, watchdog-attributable drain events, and customer-visible error codes. `tp_watchdog_enabled` is ON for Dedicated canary only (default OFF in Hosted).

**Timeouts to start with (conservative, to avoid false positives):**
- ADR-0127 initial defaults: **decode step 15,000 ms; prefill step 60,000 ms; collective 10,000 ms**, to be tuned per model/hardware from perf-canary data.
- The two-stage soft/hard config actually proposed for the canary: **decode soft 1,500 ms / hard 5,000 ms; prefill soft 10,000 ms / hard 45,000 ms; collective soft 3,000 ms / hard 15,000 ms; `consecutive_hard_timeouts_to_drain: 1`**, with `decode_watchdog = max(2s, 20x EMA(decode_iter_ms))`. Only *hard* breaches drain; soft breaches are dashboard-only.

**Immediate-rollback metrics / alert conditions (false positives or drain storms):**
1. **Watchdog false positives: drain/restart events >3 per hour per cluster without a corresponding request-timeout reduction** (ENG-4829 hard stop).
2. **Widespread watchdog-triggered drains across replicas** — signals the false-positive threshold is too low or there's a systemic perf regression → immediate rollback, no debate, page runtime TL + SRE lead.
3. **Replica churn: drain/restart exceeding baseline by >2x for >30 minutes** (canary plan: drain events "not > 2x baseline, avoid thrash"). Alert ladder: **WARN >2 drains/hour in the canary cluster; PAGE >5 drains/hour, or any drains correlated with increased customer-visible timeouts.**
4. **p99 latency regression >10% sustained >2 hours** vs baseline (ENG-4829 rollback), escalating to **>20% sustained 15+ minutes with customer impact** (checklist immediate rollback); throughput drop >5% at steady load.
5. **Customer-facing signal:** customer-visible 5xx/timeout rate up **>0.5% absolute** for canary accounts over 60 minutes attributable to runtime; Dedicated paging gate **STREAM_TIMEOUT >1.0% for 5m** (vs WARN 0.5%/5m, PAGE 2.0%/5m with heartbeat-gap correlation).
6. **Hard NCCL error spike** correlated with sync hardening and absent in baseline, or a **new deadlock/hang signature** (no drain, no abort, heartbeat stalls across ranks), or any repeatable hang where replicas wedge and don't recover via drain within 10 minutes.

On the alerting side, page on **hard watchdog abort rate**, not soft-exceeded (soft is dashboard-only), and enable drain-event dedupe/rate-limits (PR-21921) so per-rank drain events don't manufacture a fake drain storm. If false positives are suspected, the prescribed action is to disable `tp_watchdog_enabled` while keeping stall-detection metrics on; if a perf regression is suspected, first disable `tp_nccl_stream_sync_hardening` and keep the scheduler guardrail on.

## Answer

**Enforcement difference.** An *incompatibility* is enforced per-request at resolution time: the policy engine (source of truth) plus the runtime evaluate model/hardware/runtime/request-shape/availability constraints, and on a hard incompatibility the profile "must fallback" to baseline with a machine-readable reason (`GPU_UNSUPPORTED`, `MAX_CONTEXT_EXCEEDED`, `REQUEST_SHAPE_UNSUPPORTED`, `PROFILE_NOT_PUBLISHED_IN_REGION`, `PROFILE_ARTIFACT_INTEGRITY_FAILED`, `KILL_SWITCH_ENABLED`, …). The route config still references the profile, the outcome is `res=fallback` with `quant_profile_id=<requested>` plus `quant_fallback_reason`, and it is expected/self-healing — nothing was "turned off".

A *quality-regression* block is not a runtime capability judgement at all. It is an explicit, operator-authored control-plane guardrail: a **known-bad block entry** (scoped to `model_id` + `variant` + `quant_profile_id` + `profile_version`) added to the quantization profile constraints/allowlist consumed by the policy engine, so the profile "cannot be applied … even if referenced in route config". Resolution is deterministic — baseline precision with an explicit **blocked** reason — and "blocked" is deliberately tracked as a **distinct outcome from "incompatible"** so it alerts/observes separately (metrics tag `quant_profile_resolution=blocked` + audit trail) and surfaces operator remediation text ("Profile blocked due to quality regression; use default precision or select qp_int8_calib_v2"). It is durable against re-enablement (route-level disable alone is "necessary but not sufficient (humans/automation can re-enable)") and narrower than the global kill switch. SUP-27411 makes the contrast explicit: the incident "is not an incompatibility fallback issue; requests were deterministically applying the profile" — the fix was to block publication/use of the profile on the variant, not to change hardware/request compatibility. Operationally the block takes effect for existing routes "on next config cache refresh".

**Oncall verification that a customer route is back on baseline.**
1. **Confirm the write landed**: route update returned HTTP 200 / Console "Saved" after setting `quantization_profile_ref` to `"default"` (or "Disabled"); audit logging must be enabled.
2. **Logs/traces (what is actually being applied)**: query the serving-runtime request logs / trace span tags `route_id`, `tenant_id`, `model_id`, `quant_profile_id`, `quant_resolution_outcome`, `quant_fallback_reason` for the customer's route in a recent window. Within ~30–90 s of propagation and certainly within 5–10 min, `quant_resolution_outcome` must be `disabled` (not `applied`, and not `fallback`) and `quant_profile_id` must be absent/`none`/null. Re-check the customer's post-rollback request IDs; if the attrs are missing entirely you may be on an older runtime build or the request never hit the model runtime.
3. **Dashboards** (Console → Observability → Quantization Profiles, "Quantization Profile Rollout" dashboard, filtered to the route/tenant/time window): `enabled_routes` for that route → 0; `fallback_rate` by route/reason drops if the incident was incompatibility/artifact-loading driven (it can stay flat if unrelated); p95 latency returns toward baseline (within ~5% of pre-incident); 5xx back to normal within 10–15 min; token-cost delta returns to baseline.
4. **Audit history / change-control evidence**: query audit events of type `route.quantization_profile.updated` (and `quant_profiles.kill_switch.updated` if the global switch was used) filtered by `route_id` around the request timestamp, and capture `actor`, `tenant_id`, `route_id`, `old_value`/`new_value`, `timestamp`, change source (API/Console) — i.e. the diff showing `quantization_profile_ref` → `default`. These structured events (actor identity + normalized diff, exportable to SIEM, also visible in the Console route changelog) are what you hand a customer asking "who changed it / prove we're on baseline"; for tenant-wide overrides the runbook requires "Confirm audit log emitted and exportable (required for regulated customers)".
5. **If it isn't taking effect**: re-check the update succeeded, then propagation health — config cache refresh latency and policy engine config snapshot version — and if propagation is stuck with ongoing impact, escalate to Step 3 (global kill switch), where the expected outcome is likewise `quant_resolution_outcome=disabled` with a kill-switch reason (disabled, not fallback).

## Concise answer

**Current suppression rules:** (a) intent-only signals cannot create HubSpot tasks unless confidence ≥0.85 with an explicit request, or intent is combined with a real threshold signal (default routing floor is confidence ≥0.70); (b) "vanity intent" — a bare pricing-page or docs-homepage view — never routes, and docs/pricing intent needs ≥1 high-intent action (security FAQ, dedicated/private docs, DPA/SOC2 click, contact-sales); (c) intent must be sustained (≥2 events across ≥2 days in 7d, or 2+ intent events in 7d / 1 intent + a threshold signal); (d) internal/test orgs are hard-denied and scale signals need sustained volume; (e) open-task suppression (open router task created within 14 days → note only), marketing high-touch suppression, opt-out/DNC, false-positive disposition, and idempotency on `company_id + signal_type + signal_window_end_date`.

**Cooldown windows:** ADR — 30 days security/compliance intent, 14 days spend-velocity/scale, 7 days reliability/429/latency, per company + signal_type (a meaningfully distinct signal_type may still fire). ENG-7801 TTLs — 14 days default, 7 days reliability, 21 days compliance intent. Plus 14 days after "customer requested no sales outreach," 30 days after a false-positive disposition, 60–90 days on an AE "Not interested / research only" outcome, 90-day DNC minimum, and 14 days of marketing suppression after a sales task is created.

**Why this prevents a repeat of Quartz Commerce:** Quartz was routed at score 0.72 on intent alone with zero product usage. Post-fix, that same signal is blocked at three independent points — it fails the ≥0.85 intent-only confidence bar, it is vanity intent without an explicit request or combined threshold signal, and it fails the baseline-activity gate (`tokens_last_14d == 0` → no AE task). Even if a later signal fired, the DNC/opt-out properties, the 30-day false-positive suppression, the open-task rule, and the per-signal-type cooldowns downgrade it to a timeline note instead of a task, with the reason recorded (COOLDOWN / OPEN_TASK / MARKETING_HIGH_TOUCH / INTERNAL_ORG) for audit. ENG-7801's acceptance criteria state the goal explicitly: "Quartz Commerce false-positive class is mitigated by vanity-intent suppression and/or confidence threshold."

## Answer

**Recover first (forward-fix), roll back only if the migration is confirmed non-reversible.**

**Operator recovery path for a Postgres migration lock timeout:**
1. **Pause and capture evidence before touching anything** — installer log excerpt at "Running migrations", migration job/pod status + `describe` + last 200–500 log lines, `kubectl get events` tail. Do **not** restart the crash-looping job before capturing logs, and never do direct DB manipulation (e.g. deleting lock rows) from Support.
2. **Confirm the signature**: `ERROR: canceling statement due to lock timeout` / `migration failed: timed out acquiring advisory lock` in `job/redwood-control-plane-migrate`, plus long-running Postgres transactions from a stale control-plane worker.
3. **Scale control-plane deployments to 0** (`redwood-control-plane-api`, `redwood-console`) to release stale connections, keeping the data plane serving to minimize blast radius.
4. **Find and kill the blocker**: query `pg_stat_activity` ordered by `now()-xact_start`, then `select pg_terminate_backend(<pid>);`.
5. **Re-run the migration job** — delete the failed job pod and re-apply the hook (or `helm upgrade --reuse-values`). If still blocked, restart the Postgres pod as the last escalation.
6. **Scale control plane back up and verify**: `kubectl rollout status deploy/redwood-control-plane-api`, check for `CrashLoop|Error`, confirm version endpoints report the target version.

**Rollback path:** use the installer's deterministic rollback — `redwood-private rollback --upgrade-id <ID> --wait` (or `redwood-private upgrade rollback --state-dir <path> --output rollback-report.json`), which consumes stored upgrade state, runs rollback hooks in reverse order, reconciles Helm releases to prior pins, and runs post-rollback health checks. **But**: some DB migrations are not safely reversible, so if the state marks the migration stage non-reversible or rollback is blocked, the authoritative path is **restore from backup** (stop/scale CP writes → snapshot/logical restore → restore config/state → reconcile Helm to pre-upgrade pins → re-verify). Per the customer-facing ladder this is staged: soft revert → canary redeploy to prior pin → cluster slice revert + traffic shift → snapshot restore (last-known-good) + full evacuation, each with abort criteria and an owner. Support must never advise a version downgrade without Platform → Private Deployments approval.

**Upgrade artifacts to capture for change management** (retain ~30 days internal; 90 days / contract-aligned for regulated): the **upgrade plan** (`plan.json` + human summary, stored in the change ticket — target versions, environment metadata, ordered stages, per-stage rollback entry points, required artifacts + integrity checks, required approvals/gates), **precheck report**, **backup report + backup identifiers**, **upgrade execution report** / installer state-machine logs, **rollback report** if used, sanitized **installer logs** and referenced **artifact manifests** (digests/signatures), a **support bundle with upgrade trace** (`redwood-private support-bundle --include-upgrade-trace`), plus the migration-job logs and `pg_stat_activity` diagnostics from the incident, and the change-management evidence pack (release-gating checklist PDF, upgrade E2E matrix, nightly E2E run, approval sign-off, comms template, maintenance-window confirmation). Secrets, private keys/KMS material and full DB dumps must not be collected.

**Audit events to capture:** upgrade started, prechecks pass/fail, backup started/completed (or failed), apply/upgrade stage started/completed/failed, migration step outcomes, and rollback invoked/completed/failed — with step-level detail, not just start/stop. Each event should carry `event_id`, `event_type`, `event_version`, `occurred_at`, `environment_id`/`cluster_id`, a stable `upgrade_id`, `initiated_by` + `initiated_by_type` (SSO user vs service account), `request_source`/`client_ip`, `source_version`→`target_version`, `result` + `error_code`/`error_summary`, `artifact_digests`, `backup_id`/`backup_result`/`backup_location_ref`, and `rollback_reason`/`rollback_target_version`. Events come from the control-plane API and locally from the installer (stdout + local file, forwarded when connected), and must be exportable/forwardable to the customer's SIEM for long retention (e.g. 400 days) with tamper-evidence.

## Answer

### 1. The standardized template telemetry header format

The format being standardized is a **fixed, allowlisted set of low‑cardinality `x-redwood-template*` request headers** sent by the quickstart/DevEx templates and whitelisted + validated at the API gateway edge.

**The v1 allowlist** — `pr-18421-add-template-telemetry-header-whitelist` · §2 · p1:

> "Allowed headers (v1): `x-redwood-template-id` (e.g. `rag-agent`), `x-redwood-template-version` (semver like `0.3.1`), `x-redwood-template-lang` (`python`|`typescript`), `x-redwood-template-origin (`cli`|`github`), `x-redwood-template-otel` (`enabled`|`disabled`)."

**Why it exists (KPI tracking)** — same chunk, §2 · p1:

> "Context: DevEx quickstart templates need a reliable, low-cardinality way to tag traffic as template-generated so we can measure activation funnel and time-to-first-success without relying on parsing user-agent strings. Today the API gateway drops unknown `x-*` headers by default; templates adding a telemetry header would silently lose that tag."

> "Operational notes: This is required for the Quickstart Templates KPI dashboard (PM-912)."

**Validation / shape of the format** — §2 · p1:

> "Validation rules: values must match `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]{0,63}$` (lowercase enforced), max length 64, no whitespace, no commas/quotes/newlines. `x-redwood-template-version` is additionally checked as semver-like `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` with an optional `-prerelease` suffix. Any header not in the allowlist continues to be stripped by default."

> "What this does: Adds a `template telemetry` header allowlist and validator at the gateway edge. Allowed headers are normalized into a structured internal context object that can be consumed by downstream logging/metrics/analytics (follow-up PRs). Invalid values are rejected with a 400 (clear error message)…"

The originating design thread settled on the same naming and the "gateway translates to internal tag" model — `1740741199-template-telemetry-tagging-and-privacy` · §2 · p1 (Logan Wright):

> "Also: event pipeline prefers something like `x-redwood-template: rag-agent` and `x-redwood-template-version: 0.3.1`. Then gateway translates to an internal tag in request context."

…and §2 · p3 (Monica Patel): "headers: `x-redwood-template`, `x-redwood-template-version` / internal metric dimension: `redwood.template`".

### 2. Default behavior when a corporate proxy blocks the headers

**Originally the templates sent the headers by default, and a strict proxy made the request fail outright before it ever reached Redwood** — `SUP-29458-template-telemetry-header-blocked-by-corporate-proxy` · §3 · p1:

> "When using the Quickstart template defaults (telemetry tagging enabled), requests include one or more template-origin telemetry headers. Northbridge's corporate proxy rejects requests containing unapproved custom headers, returning HTTP 400/431 before the request leaves their network. Removing the custom header(s) makes requests succeed immediately."

§9 · p2: "Status: 431 Request Header Fields Too Large (sometimes 400 Bad Request) … Error text: 'Request rejected: header not allowed' / 'Unknown header: X-Redwood-Template'"; §8 · p1: "Proxy rejects request when template telemetry headers are present. Request never reaches Redwood gateway."

**The product decision was therefore to make the headers opt-in — by default the templates emit nothing, so a blocking proxy is a no-op** — `SUP-29458` · §12 · p2 (Decision / resolution):

> "Default templates will NOT send template telemetry headers unless explicitly enabled."
> "Gateway will continue to allow/validate a small set of telemetry headers (for opt-in users), but templates should not emit them by default."
> "Decision (DevEx + PM + Gateway): make template-origin telemetry tagging opt-in."

§15 · p3: "Product decision: telemetry headers from templates will be opt-in going forward to avoid corporate proxy incompatibilities." §13 · p2: "Set template telemetry to disabled (default in upcoming template release)."

**The opt-in mechanism** is a boolean env var, per `1740741199-template-telemetry-tagging-and-privacy` · §2 · p2:

> "Monica/Dana: implement opt-in boolean env var `REDWOOD_TEMPLATE_TELEMETRY=1` that adds fixed headers."

with the TS scaffold gating the headers on `process.env.REDWOOD_TEMPLATE_TELEMETRY === '1'`, and Marcus Lin: "Default should be OFF. That's the cleanest privacy stance." The gateway PR confirms the templates keep the headers behind a flag: "template repos will keep sending these headers behind an opt-in flag to avoid issues with restrictive corporate proxies" (`pr-18421…` · §2 · p1).

**Mitigation if you do want the tags behind such a proxy** — `SUP-29458` · §13 · p2: "If customer later wants telemetry tagging for internal KPIs, coordinate with network/security to allowlist the header(s) or use a non-header mechanism (future enhancement)." And `quickstart-templates-project-brief` · §18 · p4: "| Telemetry headers blocked by corporate proxies | Requests fail; adoption metrics incomplete | Make telemetry opt-in; fall back to query param or SDK tag where possible; document workaround |".

**In one sentence:** the standard is a small, strictly-validated allowlist of `x-redwood-template-*` headers (`-id`, `-version`, `-lang`, `-origin`, `-otel`) that the gateway normalizes into an internal tag for the Quickstart Templates KPI dashboard (PM-912); because strict corporate proxies hard-fail those requests with 400/431 before they reach Redwood, quickstart templates do **not** send them by default — telemetry tagging is opt-in via `REDWOOD_TEMPLATE_TELEMETRY=1`, so under a blocking proxy the default template simply sends no telemetry headers and works normally (with adoption metrics undercounted by design).

### Answer

**Root cause:** a deduplication bug in the usage exporter — it counted retried streaming chunks as separate completions whenever the request id changed across retry boundaries, inflating output-token totals in the usage aggregation pipeline and the daily export files. The hosted API and billing were untouched because invoice generation reads a separate, validated counter. The bug went unnoticed by monitoring because there was no reconciliation check between the invoice counter and the export counter.

**Mitigation taken:** export generation was paused at 18:05 UTC (first customer ticket 16:03, pipeline team engaged 16:21), the affected data was backfilled after the fix, and exports resumed with corrected logic at 22:10 UTC. Impact was limited to 17 customer workspaces with bad export rows for roughly 6 hours; no invoice corrections were needed.

**Follow-up steps to prevent a repeat (3 action items):**
1. Per-workspace, per-day reconciliation job between invoice counter and export counter, paging on drift > 0.5% (Eng SRE) — closes the detection gap.
2. Fix the exporter's dedup logic to key on a stable trace id that survives retries (Eng Platform) — removes the root cause.
3. Add a contract test in the usage pipeline covering streaming retry semantics (Eng Platform) — guards against regression.

**Root cause: a leading UTF‑8 BOM (0xEF 0xBB 0xBF) glued onto the first group name in the comma‑separated `groups` attribute, which the group splitter never stripped.**

**The parsing problem**

The customer's IdP exports group membership as a *single* CSV string in one `groups` SAML attribute, and the role mapping keys off the first matching group:

> "Customer reported that after onboarding to Private VPC (prod-us-east) a subset of their admin users suddenly lost admin privileges and received 403s from the Admin Console APIs. The customers use a SAML IdP (OnPrem SAML 2.0) that sends a 'groups' SAML attribute exported as a single CSV string containing group names." — §3, p1

> "- - Redwood Private (customer-managed control plane) deployed in VPC (us-east-1) … - - Role mapping configured: first matching group name -> Admin role" — §5, p1

After the connector upgrade, the attribute's first byte sequence was a BOM, so the first token was not the bare group name:

> "- - Server-side logs show groups attribute present but first group value appears empty when parsed by our role-mapper. Example raw attribute (hex): \"EF BB BF 63 72 65 73 74 6C 69 6E 65 2D 61 64 6D 69 6E 73,...\" which corresponds to a leading UTF-8 BOM (0xEF,0xBB,0xBF) before 'crestline-admins'." — §7, p1

The splitter only split on comma and trimmed whitespace, so the invisible BOM survived into the compared token and the exact match against `crestline-admins` failed:

> "[2026-03-11 08:47 UTC] Arjun Patel (Auth Eng): Reproduced locally by injecting BOM into groups attribute. Our group-splitting routine uses strings.Split on comma and then TrimSpace, which does not remove the BOM. Created patch to run NormalizeUnicode(strip BOM and control chars) on attribute values before splitting." — §10, p2

> "- - BOM present when assertions originate from the customer's AD connector (Windows service). - - Other federations (Okta) do not include BOM. - - Our group parser did not sanitize Unicode control characters (BOM)." — §12, p2

Trigger and blast radius:

> "- - Customer confirmed IdP was recently upgraded and exported group values using a library that appears to inject a leading BOM on some exports (particularly from their Windows-based AD connector). - - This behavior only affects assertions coming from that connector; other users (federated via Okta) are unaffected." — §9, p2

> "[2026-03-10 11:05 UTC] Customer (Crestline SSO Admin): Uploaded sample SAMLResponse and advised this started after they patched their AD connector on 2026-03-08." — §10, p2

> "- Limited to customers whose IdP emits BOM in attributes; high impact for those relying on exact-match role mapping that considers first group or strict equality." — §13, p2

Because SSO itself succeeded and only the RBAC mapping lost the group, users authenticated and then hit 403s on admin calls (e.g. "Received 403 Forbidden from Admin API", §6, p1).

**The server-side patch**

> "Auth Eng deploved patch y1.14.3 to customer's private control plane: attribute normalization step added to SAML attribute processing (strip leading/trailing Unicode BOM and common invisible chars, then TrimSpace). Unit tests added to cover BOM, ZWNBSP, and other left-to-right marks." — §14 (resolution), p2

So the fix inserts a normalization stage **before** the comma split: strip leading/trailing Unicode BOMs and other invisible/control characters, then TrimSpace, with new unit tests for BOM, ZWNBSP and left-to-right marks (tracked in `github.com/redwood-inference/auth/pull/5123`, §1, p1). Rollout was confirmed on 2026‑03‑12: "Confirmed patch rollout to their private cluster restored admin role for previously affected users. No further 403s observed for those accounts." (§10, p2). Interim workarounds were a secondary mapping matching the literal BOM‑prefixed group, or making the IdP normalize attribute values before export (§8, p1).

## Answer

**Cause:** The identity-proxy's performance cache of role assertions, keyed by the SAML `session_index`. The `session_index` is stable across IdP group syncs, so the cached role set for an already-authenticated session was never invalidated — the user's existing session kept resolving to their **pre-sync (old) roles** until the cache expired (60s TTL on that private deployment). Because the cache was per-proxy-instance, requests that hit a cache HIT got the stale, insufficient role set and were denied (`no-matching-role-after-eval` → 403), while requests that missed the cache did a live lookup and were allowed — hence the intermittency. Logging out/in forced a fresh SAML assertion and a new cache entry, which is why it fixed it. Audience mismatch, clock skew, cookie and TLS issues were explicitly ruled out.

**Mitigation applied:** (1) targeted session revocation via the Admin API for the impacted admin accounts (plus telling affected users to re-authenticate), and (2) temporarily lowering the session-index cache TTL from **60s to 5s** in the customer tenant during their next scheduled IdP sync window to shrink the stale-decision window.

**Long-term server-side fix:** Merged a **cache-eviction path triggered by identity-change (IdP user-change) webhooks, enabled by default for private deployments** (PR redwood-inference/platform#4892; also a feature flag to reduce session-index cache TTL in private tenants). Follow-ups: monitor post-deploy and update the SSO runbook with guidance for large IdP group changes (rolling sync or pre-emptive cache purge).

When those handoffs occurred the stream would resume but the final application-level 'end' chunk was missing and the client received one or more duplicated heartbeat frames."* Repro (§3) used *"an edge load balancer (tcp RST after 30s idle)"*, then *"the terminal 'end' event does not arrive but heartbeat frames are duplicated and prefixed to resumed payload."*

- **Investigation (§6):** *"ordering not guaranteed when upstream socket closed mid-flush"*; the gateway *"retransmitted heartbeat while serving-runtime was simultaneously finalizing the stream"*, aggravated by the client's immediate resume with `last_seq`.

**Root cause (§7 root_cause, p1, verbatim):** *"Race condition in sse-gateway where in-flight terminal chunk flush and scheduled keepalive/heartbeat could be interleaved after a mid-flight upstream TCP RST, leading to the terminal 'end' event being dropped under tight resume timing."*

**Server-side fix (§8 resolution + §9 resolution_notes, p1–2):** *"Rolled out inference-runtime PR 2147 which ensures atomic terminal event emission and orders heartbeat frames behind terminal flush. Nimbus confirmed no further truncated sessions after 12 hours (§5, 2026-03-12 02:45 UTC).

**Concise answer:** The root cause was a race in `sse-gateway`: after a brief upstream TCP RST, the in-flight terminal-chunk flush and the scheduled keepalive/heartbeat were interleaved, so the heartbeat got retransmitted (duplicated) and the terminal `end` event was dropped under tight resume timing. The fix was server-side PR 2147 in `inference-runtime`/`sse-gateway`, which makes terminal-event emission atomic and orders heartbeat frames behind the terminal flush — the flush path now waits for the terminal payload write to complete before accepting a resume for the same `session_id`, with a ~250 ms server-side resume window/backoff to absorb in-flight socket tear-downs (canary 2026-03-11, full rollout 2026-03-12).

## Incident Bot v2 — break‑glass reads of tenant‑scoped config diffs & privileged telemetry

### 1) Audit events that MUST be emitted

The canonical taxonomy is in **`incident-bot-access-audit` · §12 "h2. Required events"** (all events are in the *Audit Event v3* central schema, §11):

> `|| Event name || Trigger || Notes ||`
> `| incident_bot.config_diff.read | Bot requests a config diff for a tenant/workspace/environment. | Emitted even when diff is empty (to show access). |`
> `| incident_bot.config_diff.denied | Bot request is denied by authz policy. | Must include policy decision reason code. |`
> `| incident_bot.telemetry.query | Bot issues a privileged telemetry query (GPU/queue/KV cache/etc.) for incident context. | Must include query class + boundedness metadata (not raw query). |`
> `| incident_bot.telemetry.denied | Telemetry query denied by policy. | Include reason code + required scope. |`
> `| incident_bot.break_glass.activate | Break-glass flow is initiated and granted. | Must include approver mechanism (policy rule) and expiration. |`
> `| incident_bot.break_glass.deactivate | Break-glass expires or is revoked. | Include reason (expired/manua revoke). |`

Break‑glass specifically (§10 "h2. Break-glass", p.2): *"Break-glass access is allowed only for Sev0/Sev1 and requires additional audit events (see Event taxonomy)."* And (§17, p.5): *"All privileged calls made under break-glass must include \*break_glass=true\* and \*break_glass_session_id\*."*

So a break‑glass config‑diff read emits **`incident_bot.break_glass.activate` + `incident_bot.config_diff.read`** (or `...config_diff.denied`), and a break‑glass telemetry read emits **`incident_bot.break_glass.activate` + `incident_bot.telemetry.query`** (or `...telemetry.denied`), with **`incident_bot.break_glass.deactivate`** on expiry/revocation. On audit‑pipeline failure, §17 adds: *"Emit incident_bot.privileged_call.failed with reason "audit_unavailable" where possible."*

Corroborating implementations:
- **`pr-29133-add-audit-events-for-bot-access` · §2 (p.1)**: *"New audit event schema `audit.event.v1` with two event types: `incident_bot.config_diff.read` and `incident_bot.telemetry.query (plus `*.denied`)… Events are emitted for both allow and deny outcomes."*
- **`pr-29140-rollout-config-diff-permissions` · §2 (p.1)**: *"Emits audit config diff access on every reguest and audit breakglass arant when break-glass is used (fields: incident id. severity, tenant id hash. actor, client id, reason, slack channel id. slack_thread_ts, grant_ttl_seconds, decision). These align with the audit event schema added in PR-29133."*
- **`ENG-5426-incident-bot-permissioning-and-scopes` · §5/1 "2) Audit events" (p.1)** names the tentative set `incident_bot.config_diff.read_redacted`, `incident_bot.telemetry.query.read_safe`, `incident_bot.break_glass.grant`, `incident_bot.break_glass.revoke`, `incident_bot.access.denied`, and §9 requires *"Audit events emitted for every privileged call (allow + deny), visible in audit log pipeline (SIEM ingestion verified)"* and *"do not sample break-glass grants"* (§11).

### 2) Retention — SIEM vs immutable archive

**`incident-bot-access-audit` · §17, "h2. Primary retention policy" (p.4)**:

> `- *SIEM (searchable):* 400 days retention for all incident-bot privileged access events.`
> `- *Immutable archive:* 7 years retention in WORM/immutable storage (for compliance evidence and customer contractual obligations).`

Confirmed by the doc's Change log (p.5): *"2025-05-06: Updated retention (400 days SIEM searchable + 7 year immutable archive) and added fail-closed guidance for audit pipeline outages."* Storage is region‑aligned, and *"EU-scoped tenant events must remain within EU data residency boundaries for the archive"*; SIEM index access is itself audited.

(Note: the earlier approval thread only said retention was *"aligned to current internal standard"* / *"same retention policy as other privileged reads"* — the 400‑day/7‑year figures come from the audit spec above.)

### 3) Baseline vs break‑glass permission scopes

**Baseline (always‑on, least privilege)** — `20250212-incident-bot-permissions-audit-approval` · §2 (p.1): bot runs as service identity **`svc-incident-bot`** with *"Two new internal scopes"*:
- **`incident_bot:config_diff:read`** — *"(customer-safe, redacted output only)"*
- **`incident_bot:telemetry:read_privileged`** — *"(bounded query templates; tenant-aware guardrails)"*
- *"No write scopes. No direct access to raw secret stores."*

Equivalent names elsewhere: `config.diff.read_redacted` / `telemetry.query.read_safe` / `deploy.metadata.read` (ENG‑5426 §5); in code, service scope **`configdiff:read_redacted`** and interactive permission **`config.diff.read_redacted`** gated by role `platform-oncall` or `sre-oncall` (pr‑29140 §2). Audit payloads record `permission_scope: config:diff.read_redacted` and `permission_scope: telemetry:query.privileged` (incident-bot-access-audit §17).

**Break‑glass (Sev0/Sev1 only)** — `pr-29140-rollout-config-diff-permissions` · §2 (p.1):
> *"Added endpoint path `POST /v1/config/diff:breakglass` which returns the same redacted diff but allows bypassing the normal role check when ALL of the following are true: request includes `incident_id`, `severity` in {SEV0, SEV1}, `oncall_user` (from OIDC), and `slack_channel_id` + `slack_thread_ts` for correlation; caller has base scope `breakglass:request` (limited to SRE tooling identities) and is in the on-call group (Pager duty group sync) OR is a member of `sre` org team; break-glass grant is time-bounded (15 minutes) and rate-limited per incident/user."*

Crucially, break‑glass **widens who may read, not what is returned**: *"Break-glass does NOT change redaction behavior; it only changes who can retrieve the redacted diff. (Unredacted diff remains an internal-only admin workflow outside of Slack/incident-bot.)"* — echoed in ENG‑5426 §8: *"even then, do not allow secrets (keep existing redaction patterns + allowlists)"*, and §7 out-of-scope: *"Allowing raw config secret retrieval via the bot (never allowed)."*

⚠️ **Discrepancy in the corpus on grant TTL**: pr‑29140 §2 says the grant is *"time-bounded (15 minutes)"*, whereas `incident-bot-access-audit` §17 (p.5) states *"Break-glass is time-boxed (default 60 minutes; max 4 hours)."* Both figures are reported as written; the corpus does not reconcile them.
